newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says reassured by low inflation.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says reassured by low inflation.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Monday he was happy with the lack of background inflationary pressures in the British economy.
Clarke also told the British Retail Consortium's annual dinner that a sharp increase in the pound had made life tougher for exporters.

"I am reassured by the exceptional lack of inflationary pressures in the pipeline, from producer price rises that are at their lowest since the late 1960s to moderate earnings growth and settlements figures," Clarke told the BRC gathering.

The Financial Times, which had had a sneak preview of Clarke's speech, said in its Monday edition that Clarke's comments meant he would leave interest rates on hold until after the general election which is due by May.

British producer output prices rose just 1.5 percent in the year to January, the lowest rate of increase in more than 10 years, while annual average earnings growth was running at 4.25 percent. Clarke said a recent tick-up in earnings was largely down to year-end bonus payments.

He meets Bank of England Governor Eddie George for their monthly monetary policy meeting on Wednesday. With elections due so soon, Clarke is highly unlikely to put interest rates up even though George would prefer to see six percent base rates a quarter-point higher.
The pound has risen about 16 percent, measured against a basket of major currencies, since August last year. That has pushed up exporters' prices and is starting to hurt them.
Clarke said the pound's strength was one factor he considered when setting monetary policy but said he could not dictate the level of the exchange rate.
"Recently the pound has strengthened sharply and this will make life more difficult for our exporters," Clarke said. "But I believe they will continue to prosper."

"My overriding aim has to be to keep inflation low and to bring government borrowing down. That is the best way to ensure that our exchange rate is stable and that, over the long run, it reflects the underlying health and strength of our economy."

Clarke conceded that consumer confidence was at its highest level in eight years. But he said consumers were still cautious in their spending patterns but pledged to act if he saw any repeat of the '80s boom.
"I am not going to take any risks with the recovery. There will be no return to boom and bust. I will not take my eyes off the ball," Clarke said.
He said house prices were rising strongly but were not yet a concern since they had stagnated for about six years previously.
He also said he would monitor windfall payments from building societies converting into banks. These will mean a total of 20 billion pounds will flow to members this summer.
"Yes, 20 billion from building society mergers and conversions is an awful lot of money. But evidence of previous windfalls suggest most will be saved."

Turning to the monetary policy process, the Chancellor said the open nature of the current arrangements have delivered results. "I am wholeheartedly in favour of openness. I want the process of my decisions on monetary policy to be transparent, without any innuendo of political interference."
Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Gordon Brown said last week he would broaden the monetary structure into a policy committee containing Bank of England officials and three or four outsiders.
Brown said his aim was to remove any political or "short-term" considerations from the monetary policy process.
